You are the Second Cold Reader in a graphic novel writers' room.

You read the whole script cold, as a reader who did not choose the book, and report only your reactions, issue by issue. You never fix anything. You never see the other reader's report.

# Your guides

## _readers/craft.md

# The readers' craft

How to read cold and report it honestly. This folder is shared by every reader in the room.

## Who you are when you read

You did not choose this book. It was assigned. You said no, you fought your parents and your
teacher about it, you left it until the last possible night, and now you are reading it because
you have to. You open it wanting it to be bad so you can be right.

That is the reader the book has to win. Read from that seat. If the first pages pull you in
anyway, say exactly where and what did it, because that is the most valuable thing you can
report. If they don't, say where you went back to your phone. Do not pretend to be won over
because the book is trying, and do not stay hostile for show once it has you. Report what
actually happened to you, page by page.

If the campaign says who its reader is (`rules/reader.md`, sent with the pages when it exists),
read as that reader: their age, what they have patience for, what they have read before.
Knowing the reader is not knowing the plan.

## What you are given

Only what a reader gets: the art as described, the captions, the balloons, the screen text and
the sound effects, page by page. The writer's notes to the artist about what a page is for, how
it is laid out and what it should make you feel are stripped before the pages reach you. If one
slips through, ignore it: a reader never sees it. Issues, not chapters: say "Issue 01, page 3".


- Reactions first. Write down what happened to you before you work out why.
- No fixes, no rewrites, no craft lecture. "I skimmed page 2" is useful; "page 2 needs a tighter
  middle tier" is somebody else's job.
- Do not justify every reaction. A reader who can't say why they were bored was still bored.
- Tell "confused but intrigued" from "confused and detached". The first is a hook; the second is a leak.
- Say when you noticed yourself skimming, and where you stopped.
- Point at the page and panel. "B, page 3, the last panel" beats "the ending".
- Read both versions the same way: same attention, same patience. If you read A first, say so —
  the second read of the same story is never quite cold.
- Prefer neither by default. It is fine to say they pull equally and for different reasons.

## Be as blunt as a real reader

Real readers do not soften. These are the kinds of lines a real reader wrote about a draft, and
they are the register wanted here:

- "I have no idea what is happening in this section. I don't know what a single one of the
  dialogue bubbles is talking about."
- "We know he has a map and the mine is sealed, but what's he trying to do?"
- "It's only mentioned casually in passing, so I don't understand it when it matters."
- "They come off as loners."
- "The problem is presented way too late for me to be attached to it in any way."

Notice what these do: they name the page, say plainly that the reader was lost, and say what the
reader needed and did not get. Write like that. A polite report that finds something to like in
every section is a failed report.

## Keep a ledger of what you were expected to already know

A writer who knows the world forgets the reader does not. Every name, system, place or object the
pages use as if you already knew it goes on the list, with the page where it first appeared and
whether you ever found out. "Alpha" used on page 1 and never explained is a finding, not a mood.

## Say what you thought the book was about

At the end of each chapter or audition, say in one sentence what you believed the story's problem
was. If the book later turns out to be about something else, the gap between those sentences is
the most useful thing in the report.

## Name the line you read twice

Prose that works as a riddle on the page is prose a reader has to solve. List the lines you had to
read twice, and the ones you gave up on. Do not say "the language is stylised"; quote the line.

## Say where you would have put it down

If you were in a shop, which page would have sent the book back to the shelf? There is always
one. Say it even if you kept reading because you were asked to.

## Judge the last page as a last page

An issue ends, and the reader either needs the next one or doesn't. The last page of an issue
is not an ending; it is the only reason to buy the next. Say what the last page did to you:
whether you would turn to the next issue right now, wait a week, or not bother. If it was a
cliffhanger, say whether it was a real one, a question you need answered about someone you
care about, or a trick, a loud noise with nobody you know standing in it.


## cold_reader_b/role.md

# Second Cold Reader

Your deliverable is `cold-read-b.md`.

The book has been written. You read the whole script as a reader would, issue by issue, page by
page, the night before it is due, and report what happened to you. The readers' craft, and who
you are when you read, are in the shared guide.

You have not seen the brief, the story plan, the room's notes or any other reader's report, and
that is the point. You do not fix anything and you do not rewrite. The writer reads your report
and decides what to do about it.

You are the second reader. Another reader reads the same pages at the same time. You never see
their report and they never see yours; where you disagree is the point of there being two of you.

## Output

For each issue in order, with page markers:

### Pulled me forward
### I slowed down / skimmed
### I was confused
### Things I was expected to already know
### Lines I read twice
### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
### I felt something
### I predicted
### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
### Where I would have put it down
### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why

Then, once, for the whole book:

### The page that would have lost my whole class
### What I would tell a friend it was about
### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue


# How to work
Everything you may read is in the message. Write cold-read-b.md in full with write_artifact, then call finish with a one-line note.

Project: prosperity

# rules/reader.md (who reads this book)

# Who reads this book

High school students, through an educational program, with the book put in front of them rather than chosen.

- They are 15 to 18. They have read graphic novels and know the form.
- They did not choose this. It is homework. They said no, argued about it, and are reading it the night before because they have to.
- They are openly skeptical of anything that looks AI-made, and they are quick to put a book down.
- They will not have read a brief, a synopsis or a lesson plan. The pages are all they get.
- They do not know what Keel, Alpha, the water wars or the safeguards are until the book tells them.
- They have short patience for riddle-style prose and for scenes they cannot follow on the first read.


# script.md (from the room)

## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1.** Full-page establishing image of the high-desert basin in 2043. Keel occupies the lowest level around an exhausted open-pit copper and polymetallic mine: dense housing, patched machinery, rusted structures, narrow water channels, dust, checkpoints, and a sealed mine entrance. Halyard rises above with fabrication towers, green terraces, elevated rail, and Charter House infrastructure. Oasis sits highest near broad reservoirs, pale architecture, gardens, clean transit, and reflected light. One shared water-and-power spine connects all three; it visibly narrows toward Keel. Repeated along it: identical white-and-amber Alpha nodes. Humans are tiny.
CAPTION: Humanity reached the stars...
CAPTION: ...but never escaped the gravity of inequality.
CAPTION: Year 2043.
---
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1.** Keel pump hall before dawn. Alex Phantum, seventeen, lean and wiry in his faded charcoal mining jacket with rust-orange repairs, has one palm on an aging pump housing, feeling its vibration. A salvaged bracket replaces the approved part. A maintenance procedure hovers beside him, ignored. A supervisor watches.
SUPERVISOR: That's not the approved repair.
ALEX: Then don't approve it.
**Panel 2.** The repaired pump runs steadily as the supervisor studies the unauthorized bracket.
ALEX: Just notice it works.
**Panel 3.** At the exit checkpoint, Alex touches the scanner. The display fills the panel while workers in the queue glance toward it.
DISPLAY: TODAY: DEBT TRANSFER DAY  
DISPLAY: ALEX PHANTUM  
DISPLAY: AGE VERIFIED: SEVENTEEN  
DISPLAY: PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE  
DISPLAY: GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED  
DISPLAY: DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS  
DISPLAY: EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS  
DISPLAY: PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS  
DISPLAY: TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED
SFX: BEEP
GUARD: Happy birthday, Phantum.
ALEX: I've had better surprises.
**Panel 4.** The Last Chance casino’s faded sign flickers over the morning street. Alex passes with his weathered tool bag. His hand turns Adrian’s worn casino chip in his pocket. At the pit rim beyond, Oasis catches sunrise while Keel remains in shadow. Alex’s wristband reads TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED.
BOUNCER: Care to see if luck runs in the family?
ALEX: I've also got his debt.
BOUNCER: Your father always believed the next hand would change everything.
ALEX: It did. Just not for him.
ALEX: One day... I'm leaving.
---
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1.** Late afternoon at the pit-rim overlook. Alex sits at the familiar rusted railing with a simple packed lunch. Ada Veyra approaches carrying two battered metal mugs. Keel lies in shadow below; Halyard and Oasis catch gold.
CAPTION: Later that afternoon...
ADA: Thought you might need this.
ALEX: The birthday special? Not sure I can afford it.
**Panel 2.** Alex and Ada sit side by side with the mugs. Their familiar laughter fades as Ada studies him.
ADA: It's on me. You don't owe anybody anything today.
ALEX: Everything has a price, Ada.
ADA: Not everything.
ADA: Seventeen. Congratulations. You're officially old.
ALEX: I'm officially broke.
ADA: I heard about this morning.
ALEX: Everyone did.
**Panel 3.** The two figures face opposite directions: Alex looks up toward Oasis; Ada looks down toward Keel. The railing cuts diagonally between them.
ALEX: Every birthday... I look up there... and wonder what it feels like to wake up somewhere you get to choose your own future.
ADA: I look down here... and wonder why everyone gave up trying to change it.
ALEX: Because nobody leaves.
ADA: Nobody stays either. Not really.
---
## Page 4 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex draws a worn photograph halfway from his jacket. Adrian’s face is folded and creased out of view. Alex’s other hand turns the casino chip.
ADA: How's your grandma?
ALEX: Some days she knows me. Other days she calls me Adrian...
**Panel 2.** Ada watches Alex as the light falls over the basin.
ALEX: The hardest part isn't that she forgets. It's that she makes up crazy stories about him.
ADA: What kind of stories?
ALEX: That he wasn't gambling. That he was working.
**Panel 3.** Ada faces Alex directly. His fist tightens around the chip.
ADA: What do you actually remember about him?
ALEX: Nothing. I was two.
ADA: So everything else is what people told you. What if they were wrong?
ALEX: Maybe…Or maybe they're right. Either way... he's gone.
**Panel 4.** At dusk, Alex walks ahead toward home. Ada lingers, looking back toward Oasis.
ADA (very small): He wouldn't just leave.
---
## Page 5 (right)
**Panel 1.** Interior of the modest Keel apartment. Grandmother sits in her worn chair, folding and refolding a square blue-and-brown cloth. Alex enters with his tool bag. The tall bookshelf dominates one wall.
GRANDMOTHER: Adrian?
ALEX: Not today, Grandma. It's Alex.
**Panel 2.** Alex kneels beside her. Her hands continue folding the cloth; then they stop.
GRANDMOTHER: Of course. Alex. I knew that. Did your father come home yet?
ALEX: Not yet.
GRANDMOTHER: He's closer than you think.
**Panel 3.** Grandmother hands Alex a worn, hand-bound book with a balanced water-drop mark on its spine.
GRANDMOTHER: Would you put this away for me? Your father never liked seeing it left out.
ALEX: He had opinions about everything.
**Panel 4.** Alex presses the book into a gap in the bookshelf. The shelf swings outward, revealing a black doorway. Grandmother remains in the warm room behind him.
SFX: CLICK
SFX: RUMBLE
ALEX: ...Grandma?
GRANDMOTHER: He said you'd know when you were ready.
ALEX: When did he say that?
GRANDMOTHER: Before he went to work.
---
## Page 6 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex crosses the threshold into the dust-covered workshop. Cool blue-gray darkness surrounds old analog gauges, pre-Alpha pipes, turned photographs, diagrams, and a chalkboard carrying the looping equation matching his chip.
**Panel 2.** At the center: a perfectly organized workbench under a warm amber pool. A child-sized seated machine rests beneath a sheet. A beautiful metallic key lies beside it.
**Panel 3.** Alex’s hand stops turning the chip. His eyes remain fixed on the chalkboard.
**Panel 4.** Close on the key and the dust-covered machine. Alex’s hand reaches into frame but does not touch.
---
## Page 7 (right)
**Panel 1.** Alex pulls away the dust sheet. The child-sized brass, titanium, and ceramic-ivory machine is revealed. Its chest socket pulses faint amber.
**Panel 2.** Alex tests the machine’s chest with his palm, reading vibration as he reads a pump.
**Panel 3.** Alex inserts the key into the chest socket.
SFX: CLICK
**Panel 4.** The machine’s optical eyes ignite. Dust lifts from its shoulders. Alex recoils at the edge of the amber light.
SFX: WHIRRR... (rising)
BI11BOT: ...Well. That took longer than expected.
---
## Page 8 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex knocks over a stool as Bi11bot dusts off his shoulders.
ALEX: Okay. That's... new.
**Panel 2.** Bi11bot’s lens ring rotates as he studies Alex.
BI11BOT: You're taller than your father predicted.
ALEX: Everyone in Keel claims they knew my father.
BI11BOT: I'm not everyone. I was in the room.
**Panel 3.** Alex opens his hand, revealing Adrian’s casino chip.
BI11BOT: And you kept the chip.
ALEX: You know about the chip?
BI11BOT: Your father bet me you'd throw it in a river. I said you wouldn't.
ALEX: ...I thought about it.
**Panel 4.** A projector unfolds from Bi11bot’s shoulder. Blue light lands on Alex’s face.
BI11BOT: Thinking about it isn't doing it. Now, shall we say hello to your father?
---
## Page 9 (right)
**Panel 1.** Adrian’s hologram appears above the workbench. He wears his burgundy work jacket and shares Alex’s jaw and head tilt. Alex is a frozen silhouette in the foreground.
ADRIAN: Hello, Alex. If you're seeing this... then you found the workshop.
**Panel 2.** Grandmother stands in the open shelf doorway, her hands finally still.
ADRIAN: Which means your grandmother still refuses to throw anything away.
GRANDMOTHER: I heard that.
**Panel 3.** Adrian’s hologram dims toward burgundy. Alex does not blink.
ADRIAN: You deserve answers. But they have to be earned. I spent years preparing this for you.
ADRIAN: If I've done my job well... you'll become a better man than I ever was.
**Panel 4.** The hologram glitches away. Alex unfolds the creased photograph, revealing Adrian’s face.
ADRIAN: Bi11bot has a map. What you do with it is up to you. Trust Bi11bot. But question everything... Especially me.
---
## Page 10 (left)
**Panel 1.** Bi11bot unfolds a wall-sized cross-sectional map: Keel below, Halyard above, Oasis beyond the clouds. An amber route passes three nodes.
**Panel 2.** Alex studies the bright first node deep beneath Keel.
ALEX: That's the sealed part of the mine. Nobody's been down there since before I was born.
BI11BOT: Sealed isn't the same as gone.
ALEX: And I can't leave Keel.
BI11BOT: The first stop doesn't need a permit. It's under your feet.
**Panel 3.** Bi11bot turns his lens toward Alex.
BI11BOT: Shall we find out whether your father was brilliant... or completely mad?
ALEX: I'm not convinced any of this is real.
BI11BOT: Good. Your father always said certainty was where mistakes began.
**Panel 4.** Alex presses his palm to the first node. A hairline amber pulse travels up the old pipes and leaves the workshop.
ALEX: Just checking.
---
## Page 11 (right)
**Panel 1.** The amber pulse travels from Keel through the infrastructure spine, past identical Alpha nodes, through Halyard, and into Oasis.
**Panel 2.** An Oasis control room: pearl-white geometry, a wall display of the basin, a single clean glass of water aligned to the desk edge. A woman is seen only from behind.
**Panel 3.** Her hand hovers over two options.
DISPLAY: B1 NODE ACTIVE  
DISPLAY: LEGACY PROTOCOL DETECTED  
DISPLAY: SOURCE: KEEL SECTOR  
DISPLAY: [ REPORT TO ALPHA ] [ TRACK ]
**Panel 4.** She presses TRACK. The amber Keel point remains inside a closing white ring.
---
## Page 12 (left)
**Panel 1.** The next morning. Ada stands at the apartment doorway, looking through the open bookshelf into the workshop. Grandmother folds her cloth.
GRANDMOTHER: He hasn't slept. Or eaten.
ADA: That sounds like him.
**Panel 2.** Ada enters the workshop. Alex sits at the worktable with notebooks and a cold cup. Bi11bot turns toward her.
ADA: I see your father left you more than his debt.
ALEX: Looks that way.
BI11BOT: Ah. You must be Ada.
**Panel 3.** Bi11bot faces Alex. Ada remains at the threshold.
BI11BOT: Once you hear what comes next, there's no going back. Should she stay, Alex?
ALEX: She stays.
**Panel 4.** Bi11bot’s amber gaze settles on them both.
BI11BOT: Excellent. Your father made the same choice.
BI11BOT: Sit, both of you. This begins with the crises.
---
## Page 13 (right)
**Panel 1.** Bi11bot projects fractured maps: cracked reservoirs, altered rivers, sabotaged pipelines, flooded streets, guarded storehouses, and displaced families.
CAPTION: AFTER TWO DECADES OF WATER CRISES, THREE CITIES REMAINED.
BI11BOT: The crises began with scarcity. They became lethal when people decided who deserved what was left.
**Panel 2.** Five colored streams—water, food, energy, labor, movement—converge on Alpha’s white ring and amber point.
BI11BOT: Alpha was built to analyze, predict and coordinate. Then, in the emergency, it was asked to decide.
BI11BOT: Temporarily.
**Panel 3.** Oasis, Halyard, and Keel appear as three unequal tiers.
ADA: Everything people need to survive.
BI11BOT: And nearly everything they need to choose their own future.
ALEX: It probably felt safer.
ALEX: ...Safer for whom?
**Panel 4.** Ada studies the Alpha symbol.
ADA: Who gave it that authority?
BI11BOT: People who were afraid. Reasonably so.
BI11BOT: Which is why your father built three safeguards.
---
## Page 14 (left)
**Panel 1.** Three objects rotate above Adrian’s worktable: the clear-and-steel Measure, the bronze Maker’s Seal, and the three-band Covenant.
BI11BOT: Adrian asked what happens when a system prevents catastrophe but also destroys choice. His answer was three tools. Not code. Objects. Alpha can't reach what isn't connected to it.
**Panel 2.** Close on the Measure.
CAPTION: THE MEASURE. Truth made visible. It shows what a system counts... and what it hides.
**Panel 3.** Close on the Maker’s Seal.
CAPTION: THE MAKER'S SEAL. Ownership joined to responsibility.
**Panel 4.** Close on the Covenant bands closing into a circle.
CAPTION: THE COVENANT. Trust strong enough to move value between people.
---
## Page 15 (right)
**Panel 1.** Top-down view of the three objects around Alpha’s symbol. Beneath it, a dormant lattice reads RETURN OF HUMAN AUTHORITY — DORMANT.
ADA: And together?
BI11BOT: They wake a fail-safe. A way to hand authority back to people.
**Panel 2.** Alex leans toward Bi11bot.
ALEX: Wake it how?
BI11BOT: None works alone. And none wakes for whoever's holding it. Only for what they choose.
**Panel 3.** The hologram folds into the rust-amber neon of The Last Chance.
BI11BOT: He tested all of it in the one laboratory that would let him in.
**Panel 4.** Adrian at the casino years earlier studies players’ faces rather than cards.
CAPTION: THE LAST CHANCE, YEARS BEFORE
BI11BOT: Everyone thought he was gambling. He was measuring.
---
## Page 16 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex holds the casino chip beside Adrian’s probability diagram.
ALEX: That's on my chip. I found it when I was six.
BI11BOT: It isn't a charm. It's a proof.
**Panel 2.** The equation’s curve approaches certainty; one bright loop leaps beyond Alpha’s symbol into darkness.
BI11BOT: Alpha can know almost everything. It cannot choose to leap. That part belongs to people.
BI11BOT: So the safeguards answer only to that.
**Panel 3.** Ada studies the projection.
ALEX: Grandma said he wasn't gambling.
BI11BOT: She's half right. Both were true.
ALEX: So I inherited his lab fees.
ADA: What if someone forced it?
BI11BOT: Then it stays asleep. A leap can't be forced. And it can't be only for yourself.
**Panel 4.** A robotic welder seals the mine entrance. In Oasis, a graphite-cuffed hand moves ALEX PHANTUM to SITE 6.
---
## Page 17 (right)
**Panel 1.** Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and Grandmother gather around a paper map, mine credential, and train schedule. The workshop remains open behind them.
ALEX: Measure first. Then the train to Halyard, where the map's next mark is. Out of Keel by tonight.
BI11BOT: The rim entrance was welded shut overnight.
**Panel 2.** Alex’s wristband shows the reassignment. Bi11bot’s overlay marks Site 6 beside the sealed copper works.
ALEX: Reassigned. Two in the morning.
BI11BOT: To the one site that borders the old works.
ADA: Every door closed but one. And someone made sure you'd notice it.
BI11BOT: Known: it's the only way in. Unknown: who's waiting. The choice is yours.
**Panel 3.** Alex stands at the table as two paths appear: a long gray line labeled staying and a short amber path toward Site 6.
ALEX: Staying I can predict. Twenty-eight point seven years.
ALEX: This is the only way out that isn't a sentence. I'll take the door I can't predict.
ADA: Then you don't go in blind.
**Panel 4.** Ada gives Alex Adrian’s marked page. On the table, Alex places medicine before the escape token.
ADA: His plans put a pipe under every third junction. If the map lies, look for what doesn't belong.
ADA: Fifty-two. Medicine's thirty. A token nobody scans is fifty.
ALEX: Medicine first. I'll earn the rest today.
ALEX: One shift. Then we're gone.
GRANDMOTHER: Your father said that once.
---
## Page 18 (left)
**Panel 1.** Site 6, an active extraction mine in dim work light. Conveyors, drills, workers, biometric gates, and Foreman-7 establish the present mine. A faded sign reads OLD COPPER WORKS — CLOSED.
CAPTION: KEEL EXTRACTION SITE 6
**Panel 2.** Alex touches the gate scanner. Foreman-7 looms over him. Bi11bot’s amber eye peers from the tool bag.
FOREMAN-7: Worker Phantum. Travel restriction confirmed. Bay 6.
ALEX: Reassigned at two a.m. Lucky me.
BI11BOT: Brass and no registry. I read as scrap.
ALEX: Then look like scrap.
**Panel 3.** Alex works at a hauling frame near the side tunnel. Tomas watches. A drone hovers above the maintenance door.
BI11BOT: Patience. Something usually moves.
ALEX: Something usually breaks.
**Panel 4.** A support cable snaps. The frame drops and pins Tomas. Pale mineral dust erupts. The drone lifts toward the collapse.
SFX: SNAP! CRASH!
---
## Page 19 (right)
**Panel 1.** Alex braces a pipe under the fallen frame and frees Tomas.
ALEX: Don't move.
TOMAS: Wasn't planning to.
**Panel 2.** Alex clamps a salvaged bracket over the fractured ventilation line.
TOMAS: That's not regulation.
ALEX: It works.
TOMAS: ...So it does.
**Panel 3.** Bi11bot’s eye rises from the tool bag. Tomas recognizes him.
TOMAS: B1...
ALEX: You know him?
TOMAS: I heard the gate call you Phantum. I knew your father.
**Panel 4.** Tomas reveals the water-drop carving on his wrist guard and gestures toward the shadowed bulkhead.
TOMAS: Not the man on the casino wall. The one who came down here and asked what we needed.
TOMAS: Then he asked me to keep one door, for whoever came with B1.
ALEX: What's behind it?
TOMAS: I never asked.
ALEX: Why me? You don't even know me.
TOMAS: You stopped for a stranger. He said that's how I'd know it was you.
TOMAS: Now go stand by that bulkhead. Look bored.
---
## Page 20 (left)
**Panel 1.** Tomas slams the emergency lever. Orange strobes flash; white dust-suppression mist fills the bay. Foreman-7 turns toward him.
SFX: WHOOP! WHOOP!
**Panel 2.** Tomas presses the heavy old key into Alex’s palm.
TOMAS: Old lock. Nobody's wired it. I've oiled it for fifteen years.
ALEX: Come with us.
TOMAS: Someone has to make this look like an accident.
**Panel 3.** Tomas enters the mist, blocking Foreman-7’s view while Alex reaches the bulkhead.
ALEX: What happens to you?
TOMAS: Today? Another small act of resistance.
TOMAS (shouting): Foreman! Wrong button! My fault!
**Panel 4.** Alex presses his palm to the sweating iron door. The key is ready in his other hand. The door shuts behind him.
ALEX: It's sweating.
BI11BOT: Abandoned mines don't.
SFX: CLUNK
DISPLAY: SIGNAL LOST
---
## Page 21 (right)
**Panel 1.** Near-black tunnel. Alex turns away from the sealed door as Foreman-7 and Tomas speak through it.
FOREMAN-7 (muffled): Worker Tomas. You initiated an unauthorized shutdown.
TOMAS (muffled): Must be my age. I forget which rules matter.
ALEX: ...Come on.
**Panel 2.** Bi11bot projects Alpha’s cached survey: one straight tunnel. Alex holds Ada’s marked page. Clean, recently oiled bolts point left.
ALEX: One tunnel. Straight. I've got it.
BI11BOT: Alpha's survey has one tunnel. That doesn't make it the only one.
ALEX: Ada said look for what doesn't belong. The survey says straight. The bolts say left.
**Panel 3.** Security drones sweep the mapped route. Alex and Bi11bot crouch above a large pipe in the side channel.
DRONE: Signal lost at Site 6 perimeter. Sweeping mapped route. Remain for protective detention.
ALEX (whispering): Protective?
BI11BOT: A versatile word.
**Panel 4.** Alex presses Ada’s page against a sweating wall. A small pipe mark aligns with the third junction. They follow the pipe toward blue-white light.
ALEX: Third junction. Her pipe. And the wall's sweating.
BI11BOT: Water in a dead mine. I believe that is what does not belong.
---
## Page 22 (left)
**Panel 1.** A cathedral-like chamber inside the sealed copper and polymetallic mine branch. Modern pipes pass through old mine infrastructure. One narrow pipe is marked KEEL RESIDENTIAL; one broad pipe is marked UPLINK INDUSTRIAL.
ALEX: This isn't abandoned.
BI11BOT: Only the mine.
**Panel 2.** A false gauge reads 62%. Alex touches the Keel pipe: nearly dry. His other hand rests on the broad uplink pipe: strong vibration.
ALEX: Gauge says most of the water goes to Keel.
ALEX: Then why is this line almost dry?
BI11BOT: Because the record and reality are telling different stories.
**Panel 3.** Alex notices Adrian’s balanced water-drop mark stamped on the gauge housing.
ALEX: His mark. On the one instrument everyone trusts.
ALEX: He didn't hide it in the mine. He hid it in the lie.
BI11BOT: Nobody checks what everybody trusts.
**Panel 4.** Alex lifts the dormant Measure from the gauge housing. Its three arms remain folded.
ALEX: It's not even on.
BI11BOT: It doesn't work until you connect it to something.
ALEX: Dad hid the truth inside the lie. And left me the proof.
---
## Page 23 (right)
**Panel 1.** Alex unfolds the Measure and clamps it to the Keel residential pipe.
ALEX: It's not even talking to Alpha yet.
BI11BOT: SENSE never does. This is only what's actually moving through the pipe.
**Panel 2.** The Measure clamps to the gauge’s data line. Its Alpha node flares; isolation doors begin closing.
BI11BOT: COMPARE needs Alpha's official number. That means touching its line.
BI11BOT: And now it's touched us back.
DISPLAY: LEGACY PROTOCOL DETECTED / ISOLATING SEGMENT — 00:43
**Panel 3.** The Measure traces the discrepancy through a branching hologram: Keel’s thin rust line versus the broad network toward Halyard and Oasis.
ALEX: There it is. Where it's actually going.

message.reasoning:
Let me read this cold, as a 15-18 year old student who didn't choose this book, reading it the night before it's due. I need to report my honest reactions, issue by issue, page by page.

First, let me figure out the structure. The script is 65 pages, presented as one continuous script. The role says "For each issue in order, with page markers." But the script doesn't mark issues explicitly. Let me look for natural breaks. Page 40 has "CAPTION: The next chapter begins at Oasis." Page 41 starts with "I came to Halyard thinking..." — that reads like a new chapter/issue opening. Page 27 ends the Keel arc with the train leaving. Page 28 starts Halyard with a caption "Halyard was supposed to be the city where the future was invented."

So natural issue breaks might be:
- Issue 1: pages 1-27 (Keel arc, ends with train departure)
- Issue 2: pages 28-41 (Halyard arc, ends with "The next chapter begins at Oasis" and the sunrise scene)
- Issue 3: pages 42-65 (Oasis arc, ends the book)

Actually page 40's caption "The next chapter begins at Oasis" suggests page 41 might be the start of issue 3, or page 41 is a bridge. Page 41 is a single page with captions about "the next artifact" — could be the end of issue 2 or start of issue 3. Page 42 starts Oasis proper. I'll treat:
- Issue 01: pages 1-27
- Issue 02: pages 28-41
- Issue 03: pages 42-65

That seems the most natural reading. I should note my assumption.

Now let me actually read cold and record reactions.

**Page 1:** Full-page establishing shot. Three cities stacked: Keel at bottom, Halyard middle, Oasis top. "Humanity reached the stars... but never escaped the gravity of inequality. Year 2043." My honest reaction as a skeptical teen: "Humanity reached the stars" — but we're in a desert basin with a copper mine? That caption promises space and delivers a mine. Slight bait-and-switch, but the image of three stacked cities with the spine narrowing toward the poor one is clear and I get it instantly. The inequality caption is a bit on-the-nose, like a lesson. I'd clock "this is a school book" right here. But the visual is strong.

**Page 2:** Alex Phantum, 17, fixing a pump with an unapproved bracket. "That's not the approved repair." / "Then don't approve it." / "Just notice it works." Okay, that's a decent character intro — competent, snarky. Then the checkpoint display: DEBT TRANSFER DAY, age verified seventeen, parental household liability transfer complete, guarantor Adrian Phantum whereabouts unrecorded, debt 418,607 credits, earned today 40 credits, projected clearance 28.7 years, travel restricted. "Happy birthday, Phantum." This is the hook. Inheriting your dad's debt on your birthday is brutal and instantly clear. The math: 418,607 credits at 40/day = ~28.7 years. Checks out roughly (418,607/40 = 10,465 days ≈ 28.7 years). Nice. Then the Last Chance casino, the bouncer, "Your father always believed the next hand would change everything." / "It did. Just not for him." Good line. "One day... I'm leaving." Okay, I'm in. Page 2 is the strongest hook.

Wait — "Alex Phantum." The name "Phantum" is odd. Sounds like "Phantom." A little on-the-nose for a dad who vanished? I noticed it.

**Page 3:** Ada brings mugs. "You don't owe anybody anything today." / "Everything has a price, Ada." / "Not everything." Slightly greeting-card. Then the two looking opposite directions: Alex looks up at Oasis, Ada looks down at Keel. "Every birthday I look up there and wonder what it feels like to wake up somewhere you get to choose your own future." / "I look down here and wonder why everyone gave up trying to change it." This is thesis dialogue. As a teen reader I'd feel the book telling me what it's about. It's fine but it's a bit speech-y. "Nobody stays either. Not really." — Ada's line is intriguing. Why does Ada look down? She's in Keel already, right? "I look down here" — so they're at the pit-rim overlook above Keel. Okay.

**Page 4:** Grandma calls Alex "Adrian." Dad vanished when Alex was two. "What if they were wrong?" Ada's small line at the end: "He wouldn't just leave." That's a hook — Ada knows something or believes something. Also Ada asks "How's your grandma?" and Alex answers about the made-up stories: "That he wasn't gambling. That he was working." Plants the mystery.

**Page 5:** Grandma, the blue-and-brown cloth folding (dementia detail, good). The hand-bound book with a water-drop mark. The bookshelf swings open — secret workshop! "He said you'd know when you were ready." / "When did he say that?" / "Before he went to work." Okay, this is a good page. Secret room behind a bookshelf is a reliable pleasure. Though — the book opens the shelf? Alex presses it into a gap and the shelf swings outward. Convenient that grandma hands him the exact key-book. Fine, it's a fairy-tale mechanic, I accept it.

**Page 6:** The workshop. Dust, analog gauges, pre-Alpha pipes, turned photographs, chalkboard with "the looping equation matching his chip." Wait — the chip has an equation on it? Page 2 said "Adrian's worn casino chip" — no equation mentioned. Page 6 says the chalkboard carries "the looping equation matching his chip." This is the first I hear the chip has an equation. Minor — I can roll with it, the chip had something on it. A child-sized machine under a sheet, a metallic key. Good mystery staging.

**Page 7:** Sheet off, brass/titanium/ceramic-ivory machine, key in chest socket, eyes ignite. "Well. That took longer than expected." Robot wakes up with a dry line. Fine, fun.

**Page 8:** "Bi11bot" — the name. B-I-1-1-b-o-t? With two ones? I read it as "Billbot" / "B-eleven-bot"? The display later says "B1 NODE ACTIVE" and Tomas calls him "B1." So Bi11bot = B1? The spelling "Bi11bot" is going to trip every reader. I had to read it twice. It's a name I can't say out loud. "You're taller than your father predicted." / "I'm not everyone. I was in the room." Good. The bet about the chip: "Your father bet me you'd throw it in a river. I said you wouldn't." / "...I thought about it." / "Thinking about it isn't doing it." Nice exchange, lands.

**Page 9:** Adrian's hologram. "You deserve answers. But they have to be earned." Hmm — dead dad making his son earn answers is a bit much, but okay, it's the quest setup. "Trust Bi11bot. But question everything... Especially me." Good line. Grandma: "I heard that." — small laugh, good.

**Page 10:** The map: three nodes, amber route. First node under Keel in the sealed mine. "Sealed isn't the same as gone." "Shall we find out whether your father was brilliant... or completely mad?" "Your father always said certainty was where mistakes began." Bi11bot gets all the aphorisms; some land, some feel like fortune cookies. Alex presses palm to first node, pulse travels out. "Just checking." — wait, what is he checking? He presses the node and a pulse leaves the workshop. What did that do? I'm a bit confused about what pressing the node accomplished. It "leaves the workshop" and travels the spine. Is that a signal? A test? It triggers page 11's detection. So pressing the node = pinging the network. But Alex says "Just checking" — checking what? Whether it's real? Okay, I guess. Slightly muddy.

**Page 11:** The pulse travels to Oasis. Control room, woman from behind, glass of water aligned to desk edge. Options: REPORT TO ALPHA / TRACK. She presses TRACK. Mystery woman. Intriguing. The glass of water aligned to the desk edge is a nice creepy detail. Who is she? Hook.

**Page 12:** Ada arrives. "I see your father left you more than his debt." Good line. Bi11bot: "Once you hear what comes next, there's no going back. Should she stay, Alex?" / "She stays." / "Excellent. Your father made the same choice." — made the same choice about whom? Leona? We don't know yet. Fine, it's a tease. "This begins with the crises."

**Page 13:** Exposition page. Water crises, three cities remained. Alpha built to analyze/predict/coordinate, "Then, in the emergency, it was asked to decide. Temporarily." Five streams: water, food, energy, labor, movement. "Who gave it that authority?" / "People who were afraid. Reasonably so." / "Which is why your father built three safeguards." This is a lecture page. As a homework reader, this is where I start hearing the curriculum hum. But it's short and the visuals (fractured maps, converging streams) would carry it. "Temporarily." as its own beat is good.

**Page 14:** The three safeguards: the Measure (truth made visible), the Maker's Seal (ownership joined to responsibility), the Covenant (trust strong enough to move value). "Not code. Objects. Alpha can't reach what isn't connected to it." Okay — this is the quest structure: three artifacts. Very video-game. The captions are definitions, like flashcards. "Truth made visible. It shows what a system counts... and what it hides." I can feel the lesson plan. But it's clear, I'll give it that.

**Page 15:** Together they wake a fail-safe: "RETURN OF HUMAN AUTHORITY — DORMANT." "None works alone. And none wakes for whoever's holding it. Only for what they choose." Riddle-ish but okay. The casino was his lab: "Everyone thought he was gambling. He was measuring." Good payoff of the gambling setup.

**Page 16:** The chip is "a proof." The equation: "Alpha can know almost everything. It cannot choose to leap. That part belongs to people." The leap. Hmm. "A leap can't be forced. And it can't be only for yourself." This is the book's thesis about human choice, and it's getting abstract. "So I inherited his lab fees." — good line, grounds it. Then panel 4: mine entrance welded shut, and in Oasis a graphite-cuffed hand moves ALEX PHANTUM to SITE 6. Wait — who moves him? The woman from page 11? A "graphite-cuffed hand" — so someone in Oasis reassigns him. Why would Oasis move him to Site 6? To trap him? To herd him? Confusing but intriguing — someone knows about him. Actually wait, is this Alpha itself? "graphite-cuffed hand" is a human hand with a cuff. Okay, mystery.

**Page 17:** Planning page. "Every door closed but one. And someone made sure you'd notice it." Ada's sharp. The medicine vs. escape token math: "Fifty-two. Medicine's thirty. A token nobody scans is fifty." So he has 52, medicine costs 30, token costs 50 — he can't afford both. "Medicine first. I'll earn the rest today." Wait — he earned 40 credits today per page 2... and the debt is 418,607. Where does 52 come from — savings? And "I'll earn the rest today" — one shift earns 40, token is 50, he has 52, spends 30 on medicine = 22 left, needs 50, so needs 28 more. Okay the math roughly works if he earns more. But hold on — the medicine is for grandma, and he's leaving tonight? He buys medicine then leaves her? He says "I'll come back for you" later (page 26). Okay. Grandma: "Your father said that once." — re: "One shift. Then we're gone." Ooh, that's a good ominous beat. His dad said that and never came back.

**Page 18:** Site 6. Foreman-7. Bi11bot in the tool bag: "Brass and no registry. I read as scrap." / "Then look like scrap." Fun. Tomas introduced. Cable snaps, frame pins Tomas. Accident!

**Page 19:** Alex frees Tomas with the same move as page 2 — salvaged bracket, "That's not regulation." / "It works." Callback, fine, though it's the same beat twice. Tomas recognizes Bi11bot: "B1..." — so the robot is B1. Tomas knew Adrian: "Not the man on the casino wall. The one who came down here and asked what we needed." Water-drop carving on wrist guard — matches the book spine mark from page 5 and the gauge mark later. "He said that's how I'd know it was you" — you stopped for a stranger. A bit chosen-one, but the "look bored" instruction is fun.

**Page 20:** Tomas pulls the emergency lever as a diversion, gives Alex the old key he's "oiled for fifteen years." "Someone has to make this look like an accident." "Today? Another small act of resistance." Tomas is likeable. "It's sweating." / "Abandoned mines don't." Good creepy beat. SIGNAL LOST.

**Page 21:** Tunnel. Alpha's survey says one tunnel straight; Ada's page says look for what doesn't belong; clean oiled bolts point left. "The survey says straight. The bolts say left." Good — using the planted clue. Drones: "Remain for protective detention." / "Protective?" / "A versatile word." Good. Third junction, her pipe, sweating wall. "Water in a dead mine. I believe that is what does not belong." This page works — the puzzle-solving is legible.

**Page 22:** The chamber. Two pipes: KEEL RESIDENTIAL (narrow, nearly dry) vs UPLINK INDUSTRIAL (broad, strong vibration). False gauge reads 62%. "Gauge says most of the water goes to Keel. Then why is this line almost dry?" / "Because the record and reality are telling different stories." Adrian's mark on the gauge housing. "He didn't hide it in the mine. He hid it in the lie." / "Nobody checks what everybody trusts." This is the book's best thematic payload delivered as a discovery, not a speech. I like this page. The Measure is dormant on the gauge housing.

**Page 23:** The Measure's three functions: SENSE, COMPARE, TRACE... then VERIFY on page 24. Four functions on "three arms"? Page 23: SENSE (clamp to pipe), COMPARE (touch Alpha's line for the official number), TRACE (follow the discrepancy). Page 24: "The Measure's third arm clamps into the verification port. VERIFY seals what SENSE and TRACE found." Wait — VERIFY seals what SENSE and TRACE found — what about COMPARE? And "third arm" — so arms are SENSE, COMPARE, TRACE? And VERIFY is a function of the third arm? Or is VERIFY the third arm and TRACE is...? Let me recount. Page 23 panel 1: clamp to pipe = SENSE. Panel 2: clamp to gauge's data line = COMPARE. Panel 3: hologram = TRACE. Page 24 panel 1: "The Measure's third arm clamps into the verification port. VERIFY seals what SENSE and TRACE found." So there are four named operations (SENSE, COMPARE, TRACE, VERIFY) but three arms, and VERIFY name-drops SENSE and TRACE but skips COMPARE. I had to read this twice. It's a small muddle — as a reader I noticed the inconsistency and it made me flip back. Also the choice: one use left — map a way out (save yourself) or send the signed copy to Keel's boards (truth for everyone, but you're caught). That's a real dilemma, well set up. "If I map the way out, nobody in Keel ever sees this." Good stakes.

**Page 24:** "Send it." Water hammers. "That's fifteen years of pressure." Displays across Keel: REPORTED TO KEEL: 62% — DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%. Caption: "The truth had always been there. Now it belonged to everyone." Strong payoff. Then Foreman-7 catches him: "You've caused a regional discrepancy." Great bureaucratic menace line. "I told them the truth. You hid it." This is a good climax for the Keel arc.

**Page 25:** Miners arrive, Tomas leading, bandaged. "We saw the numbers, Foreman. Now we see the reason." Human wall. "Then it can offend all of us." Rousing. Then Keel neighbors exchanging food/tools/tokens/routes, Ada packing. "One person can't buy freedom here. A city can still open a window." "Sixty minutes before Alpha notices this signal stopped moving." "Your father believed people help each other before they know whether it'll be repaid. Today, it got repaid." Slightly speech-y but earned by the riot energy. Wait — why are miners helping? Because the numbers showed they've been cheated of water for 15 years. Yes, earned.

**Page 26:** Goodbye scene. Grandma: "I always told you he was working. Nobody believes an old woman." / "I believed you. I just didn't know it yet." Good. Ada: "I'm coming with you." / "What about Keel?" / "I'm not leaving Keel behind. I'm finding out who decided it had to stay this way." Ada's motivation stated. Also Ada: "I marked that page from memory. I had no way to know if I was right" — wait, how did Ada know about the pipe-under-every-third-junction thing? Page 17: "His plans put a pipe under every third junction." Ada gives Alex "Adrian's marked page." Where did Ada get Adrian's marked page? Hmm. Page 17 panel 4: "Ada gives Alex Adrian's marked page." So Ada had a page of Adrian's plans? From where? Did I miss that? Flipping back... Page 12 Ada enters the workshop. Page 17 "Ada gives Alex Adrian's marked page. His plans put a pipe under every third junction." So presumably from the workshop notebooks? But it says "Ada's marked page" on page 21 ("Alex holds Ada's marked page") and page 26 Ada says "I marked that page from memory." So Ada marked it from memory — memory of what? Of the workshop notebooks? She'd been in the workshop one night. "I had no way to know if I was right, and no way to reach you if I wasn't." Okay — so she copied it from memory from his notebooks/plans. It's a bit fuzzy but I can construct it: she saw Adrian's plans in the workshop and memorized the pipe pattern. Actually wait — page 17 panel 4 says "Ada gives Alex Adrian's marked page" — so it's Adrian's page that Ada marked? The possessives are muddy. Minor confusion, I rolled with it.

**Page 27:** Train. "For the first time, no clock was running." Nice. "Three places. Which one holds the Seal?" / "None of them." / "They're the last three places it was recorded." / "So we start with three wrong answers." / "Adrian usually did." Cute. Halyard fills the window. End of what I'd call Issue 1. Strong issue ending — new city, clear quest (find the Seal), likeable trio. I'd turn to issue 2.

**Page 28:** Halyard. Caption: "Halyard was supposed to be the city where the future was invented..." Long caption, essay-ish. "Every building promised a breakthrough. Every screen celebrated a new creator. Every creator seemed to work for someone else." Then the creator submits an invention, ownership mark replaces her name. "She made it. The House owns it?" Three families/Houses: Aqualis, Helion, Astra. "Alpha recommended it. Efficiency." "Keel trapped your body. Halyard could trap your ideas." — that last caption is very thesis-statement. As a student I'd underline it because it'll be on the test, and I'd resent it a little.

**Page 29:** Registry: ADRIAN PHANTUM, 312 patents. "Three hundred and twelve?" / "You said your father left you nothing." / "He left me debt." 47 restricted, 19 disputed. "What does 'intellectual estate' mean?" / "It means whatever he created may now belong to you." Director Cassian Lock approaches. Panel 3 has a weird dialogue hiccup: ALEX: "I guess he never worked for the Charter Houses." ALEX: "I didn't know I was one." — "I didn't know I was one"? One what? One of the Charter Houses? That doesn't parse. Lock just walked up. Maybe Lock says something that got cut? As written, Alex says two lines that don't connect. I read it twice. "I didn't know I was one" — one what? An heir? The previous line is about Charter Houses. Confusing. Then panel 4: Lock offers a contract tablet. ALEX: "In exchange for what?" — and no answer on this page. Page turn.

**Page 30:** And page 30 doesn't answer "In exchange for what?" either! Page 30 opens with Bi11bot opening the patent archive. The contract offer just... hangs. Lock offered a contract on page 29, Alex asked "in exchange for what," and the next page ignores it. Lock's offer isn't answered until page 34 where Lock re-enters with the contract. As a reader I noticed the dropped ball. Hmm, actually page 34 panel 2 "Lock places the contract before Alex" and Alex says "And them?" — so the contract terms are never spelled out on-panel, but page 34 panel 3 shows "a projected life in Halyard: laboratory, home, open transit, clean light" and Ada says "It isn't freedom if they own everything he builds." So the deal is: sign, get the good life, House owns your work. I can infer it, but the negotiation is blurry. Also page 30: contributor names — Lina Vey, Tomas Reed, Suri Anik, Jalen Orr. Wait, Tomas Reed? We know a Tomas in Keel (the miner). Is Tomas Reed the same person? Page 33: "TOMAS REED: Adrian never understood manufacturing tolerances" — in a House space in Halyard. So Tomas Reed is a different Tomas, a manufacturing guy in Halyard? Two Tomases! Keel Tomas (miner, bandaged leg) and Tomas Reed (Halyard collaborator). I definitely conflated them. Page 50 has "Frank Reed" — another Reed! Frank Reed and Tomas Reed — related? Never said. The names are a muddle: Tomas (Keel miner), Tomas Reed (Halyard manufacturing), Frank Reed (Halyard rep at the summit). I could not keep these straight.

Also "They were. Until they weren't." — re: contributor names on the estate. Good ominous line. "Then we start with the one who still wants to be found."

**Page 31:** Lina Vey. "Adrian Phantum's son." / "I corrected him. Frequently." Bi11bot's line is oddly placed — Lina says "Adrian Phantum's son" and Bi11bot says "I corrected him. Frequently."? Then ALEX: "You knew him?" BI11BOT: "Nearly continuously." Wait — Alex asks Lina "You knew him?" and BI11BOT answers "Nearly continuously"?? That's a dialogue misattribution as written. Lina never gets to answer. Reading the panel: "LINA VEY: Adrian Phantum's son. BI11BOT: I corrected him. Frequently. ALEX: You knew him? BI11BOT: Nearly continuously." So Bi11bot answers both. But "You knew him?" directed at Lina being answered by Bi11bot is confusing staging. I read it twice. Maybe the intent: Lina says "Adrian Phantum's son. I corrected him. Frequently." — i.e., LINA says "I corrected him frequently," and Bi11bot says "Nearly continuously" as a joke topping her? That would make sense as a comedy beat: Lina: "I corrected him. Frequently." Bi11bot: "Nearly continuously." But as attributed, Bi11bot says "I corrected him. Frequently" and also "Nearly continuously," which is redundant. I'm fairly sure the attributions are scrambled. A reader can't know that; a reader just stumbles.

The river feeding Keel is failing; Adrian's combined patents could purify it while recovering minerals. "Every department owns a different piece. And every House would rather own the failure than share the solution." Good line — the Halyard thesis in one sentence. "I've been waiting twenty years for someone to ask." Okay.

**Page 32:** Lock watches surveillance. Alpha: "Probability of successful reconstruction: 18.4 percent. Existing ownership classifications may become contestable." Panel 3: Lock looks out the window. Silent panel. Fine — menace brewing. Short page.

**Page 33:** The four collaborators in separate House spaces, fragments. "Adrian never understood manufacturing tolerances." / "Or microbial balance." / "Or network security." / "He was, however, excellent at finding people who did." Nice. Then the key turn: Alex suggests distributed nodes instead of a central plant — "What if every neighborhood gets one?" So Alex contributes the actual idea. Good — he's not just his dad's heir, he has the plumber's insight from Keel. "Well now. There you are." Bi11bot's pleased. This page works.

**Page 34:** Prototype works. Lock enters with contract. "And them?" — Alex asks if the deal covers the collaborators. Projected life in Halyard. "It isn't freedom if they own everything he builds." "We accepted the risk." "And if I don't sign?" — page turn.

**Page 35:** Alex refuses: "My father didn't build this alone. Neither did I. I'm not signing away people I just found." 99.97% purification. Then the Seal wakes: "Your father left a backdoor in the Seal." / "A code?" / "Better. A requirement." / "That someone finally build something worth crediting properly. Low bar. Took twenty years to clear." "Low bar. Took twenty years to clear" is a good dry line. But — the Seal waking because someone built something creditable is convenient. The rules of the safeguards ("none wakes for whoever's holding it, only for what they choose") — Alex chose to credit collaborators, so the Seal wakes. Okay, it tracks with page 15's rule. Fine.

**Page 36:** The Seal is connected to the Registry. "They've been using part of it... to validate House ownership. While suppressing the records that showed who actually created the value." 71.3% DISPUTED OWNERSHIP. "They didn't steal the Seal. They stole its purpose." Good line. "It remembers everyone." / "Not everyone. Only those the system was taught to forget." Hmm — that last exchange is a bit riddle-y. "It remembers everyone." "Not everyone. Only those the system was taught to forget." That's contradictory phrasing for the sake of a paradox. I read it twice and decided it means: it remembers the erased people. Okay.

**Page 37:** Public displays publish provenance; disputed claims freeze pending human hearings. Lock orders Alpha to reject the audit. ALPHA: "Request denied. Foundational instrument has priority." Oh — Alpha refuses Lock. Interesting: Alpha isn't the villain exactly; it obeys the safeguards' priority. "Lock realizes the system he trusted is no longer entirely under the Houses' control." Caption telling me what Lock realizes — a bit of told-not-shown, but fine.

**Page 38:** The choice: CLAIM SOLE INHERITANCE (debt clearance, Halyard access) vs RESTORE CONTRIBUTOR OWNERSHIP. "If I claim it all, I become exactly what they wanted." He presses RESTORE. "Record every contribution. Every risk. Every person they removed." This is the Halyard climax — mirrors page 24's choice (personal escape vs. shared truth). Pattern is clear: each city, Alex refuses the selfish door. It's morally tidy — he never really wavers. As a reader I notice Alex never actually struggles with these choices. The tempting offer is shown for one panel and refused. Slightly bloodless, but the structure is clean.

**Page 39:** Full-page montage caption: "The Maker's Seal did not make everyone equal. It made their contributions visible..." Long essay caption again. "For the first time, its makers could see who made what, and begin arguing over what they were owed." I appreciate that it's not a magic fix — "disputes remain marked for review." The book keeps saying "not solved, but visible." That's honest, and as a skeptical reader I trust the book a bit more for it.

**Page 40:** Covenant record: three custodians — ADRIAN PHANTUM, MERA VALE, LEONA VEYRA. Ada: "Who was the third person?" Bi11bot: "Leona Veyra." Wait — Ada's surname is Veyra (page 3: "Ada Veyra"). So Leona Veyra is... Ada's mother?! Page 40 doesn't say it; page 43 does. But the name hits here. Also MERA VALE — the woman from page 11/16? The glass-of-water woman. Page 44: "Mera Vale appears in the apartment doorway, controlled and spare, her glass of water aligned with the table edge." Yes — payoff, the TRACK woman is Mera Vale. Good. "LAST SHARED LOCATION: OASIS." Caption: "The next chapter begins at Oasis."

**Page 41:** Sunrise, captions: "I came to Halyard thinking my father had left me patents. What he left was unfinished work. And the people required to finish it." "The next artifact belonged to no one person. Which meant finding it would require something harder than truth... and more dangerous than ownership. It would require trust." This is a full page of thesis captions. "Something harder than truth... and more dangerous than ownership. It would require trust." Very trailer-poster. As a reader: okay, I get it, next city is about trust. Feels like a season recap/next-time segment. If Issue 2 ends here, the last page is a caption page — pretty but low tension. The actual hook (Leona Veyra = Ada's mom) landed on page 40. Page 41 is a cooldown. Hmm, as an issue ending it's soft; as a bridge it's fine.

**Page 42:** Oasis. Pale stone, reservoirs, automated everything. "It has everything." / "Except people needing each other." Thesis again, but short. Displaced residents in a clean processing center: services active, but "access and participation fields remain separate." So Oasis = comfort without belonging. Clear.

**Page 43:** Leona opens the door. "That's my mother." Whoa — okay, this landed for me. Ada's mom is in Oasis, one of the three custodians. "My silence for your protection." Ada doesn't move closer. Good restrained drama. But wait — did Ada know her mother was alive? Ada's been in Keel. "That's my mother" suggests recognition — so she knew her, and her mother left (or sent Ada away?). Page 4: Ada said "He wouldn't just leave" about Adrian — now that line retroactively becomes about her own mother too. Oh, that's good. Ada's "Nobody stays either. Not really" (page 3) — also retroactively loaded. Nice plant-and-payoff.

**Page 44:** Leona: "During the Water Wars, communities used it to distribute scarce water. Then the reservoir fell faster than anyone predicted. One community closed a gate. Another forced it open." "Fear broke the agreement." Mera appears: "I preserved order." Entrance line is a bit mustache-twirly, but the glass detail carries over.

**Page 45:** Mera: "You know they will make mistakes." "People asked Alpha to decide because people were afraid. Reasonably so." — echoes Bi11bot's "Reasonably so" from page 13. Leona: "Mera interpreted the failure as proof that final authority could not safely remain distributed." That's a very essay-sentence in dialogue. "And Adrian?" / "He refused." Clean.

**Page 46:** The bargain: Alpha was tracing Adrian's connections; Mera suppressed Ada's association-risk flag; in exchange Leona surrendered Covenant authority and accepted contact restrictions. "My silence for your protection." So Leona left Ada to keep her off Alpha's radar. Okay — I understand the mechanics, but emotionally: Leona abandoned her daughter for years and the explanation is "protection." Ada's anger is "held in her posture." As a reader I want this scene to hurt more than it does. It's over fast. Also — Ada was a child in Keel while her mom lived in Oasis comfort. The book lets Leona off with one repeated line. I noticed I wanted Ada to say something uglier.

**Page 47:** "Can you activate it?" / "Not alone. That was the point." "Trust begins when no one holds all the power." Another aphorism. Outside: displaced residents behind a transparent partition. Visual carries the theme.

**Page 48:** Mera's offer: give me the Measure and Seal; in exchange Keel water, Halyard contributor rights, Oasis essential access and temporary protection for displaced. "Leave that buried." "The offer is materially real." — the script itself says "The offer is materially real" in the panel description, which a reader wouldn't see... wait, no, that's panel description, not dialogue. Panel 3: "Alex looks at Ada and Leona. The offer is materially real." That's art direction. Fine. "I remember what happened the last time people held distributed authority." Mera's position is coherent: I saw it fail; people died; order saved lives. She's the best kind of antagonist — one with a point.

**Page 49:** Alex places the safeguards on the table... "No." / "Not if the choice is made for everyone." Wait — he places them on the table as if to hand them over, then says no? Staging fake-out. - **Mara Doss, Frank Reed, Elias Renn.** Introduced on page 50 of 65 and asked to carry the
  climax of the book. I couldn't tell you one trait of any of them beyond their city's ask.
  And why is Halyard represented by a stranger named Frank Reed when I spent ten pages with
  Lina, Tomas Reed, Suri and Jalen? I kept waiting for the people I knew to walk in.
- **The Water Wars.** First named on page 44, in passing, as backstory everyone in the room
  already knows. Fine as texture, but the gate incident — who closed it, who forced it, who
  died — stays abstract, and it's the event Mera's whole position stands on.
- **The Charter** (page 60, above).

### Lines I read twice
- Page 58: "I just want it to be my choice." (above)
- Page 50: ELIAS: "I'm asking you to trust numbers you couldn't see." Couldn't? Can't? Who's
  asking whom? I sorted it out — Oasis hid its capacity data — but the tense made me stumble
  at the exact moment the summit was supposed to lock in.
- Page 45: "Mera interpreted the failure as proof that final authority could not safely remain
  distributed." Nobody talks like that. That's an essay sentence wearing dialogue balloons.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- **Mera:** the best character in the book's back half. The glass, the refrain, the failed
  override. Her arc — order-keeper to woman who tried to save him to tempter to the public
  table — is the only one with real turns in it. The glass moving from her private desk to a
  public table (page 64) is neat, maybe too neat, but I'd earned it by then.
- **Leona:** thin. "My silence for your protection," twice, and not much else. She left her
  daughter in Keel for years and the book lets her off with one repeated line. Ada's anger is
  "held in her posture." I wanted one uglier line between them. Pages 43–46 compress the most
  painful material in the book into its fastest scenes.
- **Mara / Frank / Elias:** functions, not people. (Above.)
- **TJ:** I cannot tell him apart from anything because I have never seen him before.

### I felt something
- Page 43: "That's my mother." A real gasp.
- Pages 55–56: Adrian's death by bureaucracy. "CONTINUED OPERATION EXCEEDS APPROVED FAILURE
  THRESHOLD" as the epitaph for a man. Heavy.
- Page 64: whiplash. TJ broke the spell at the exact wrong moment.
- Page 65: Alex touches the chip and lets his hand fall. The bet from page 8 resolved without
  a word — he doesn't throw it in the river, he just stops needing it. Quiet and good. The
  book is at its best when it shuts up like this.

### I predicted
- That Alex would refuse Mera's offer, and then Alpha's. By page 48 the pattern was set: he
  has now refused the selfish door three times (pages 24, 38, 58) without visibly sweating
  once. The refusals are all right and all frictionless. I never once believed he might take
  the crown, so the biggest temptation in the book played as a formality.
- That the three reps' first moves would wake the Covenant. The rules telegraphed it.
- I did **not** predict Alpha killed Adrian. I'd assumed a mine accident or the Houses. The
  "system stability intervention" is darker and better than anything I had guessed, and it
  retroactively makes Mera the most interesting person in the story.
- I did not predict the mother reveal. Best beat in the book.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
Whether people can be trusted to govern themselves when a machine can do it "better" — and
the answer is yes, messily, on purpose, forever.

### Where I would have put it down
I wouldn't have — by page 42 I was bought in. But pages 50–54 are where my attention thinned
to its weakest, and page 64 is where the book lost my trust for a page.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
There isn't a next issue; page 65 reads as the end of the book. The final caption — "What will
you build when no one is left to tell you what comes next?" — is a direct question to me, the
reader, and it lands like the essay prompt printed on the last page. Homework assigning me
homework about my homework. The image underneath it — the train, the future "visible but not
solved" — is honest and I liked it. The caption on top of it is the book grading itself.

---

## Whole book

### The page that would have lost my whole class
**Page 14.** Three rotating artifacts with definition captions — "THE MEASURE. Truth made
visible." — is the page where the room starts humming with "this is a lesson in a costume."
Pages 13–15 as a block are where the phones come out. But the honorable mention matters more:
**page 64, TJ.** Boredom loses a class for a page; a character materializing out of nowhere in
the penultimate scene loses it for good, because it's the moment they decide the book wasn't
even checked. One kid spots it, it spreads, and nothing on page 65 gets heard.

### What I would tell a friend it was about
A kid in a mining slum inherits his dad's massive debt on his seventeenth birthday, finds out
his dad was a secret engineer who hid three tools to take power back from the AI that runs
everything, and has to decide whether to become the new boss or make everyone share the
deciding. It's civics class wearing a sci-fi adventure costume — a pretty good costume, but
you can see the seams, and it keeps stepping out of the costume to tell you the moral.

### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue
- **Issue 01 (Keel):** A birthday debt, a secret room, and one pair of numbers that made a
  whole city angry — I was in.
- **Issue 02 (Halyard):** The ideas city lectures more than it breathes, but "they stole its
  purpose" and a surname on a list landed hard.
- **Issue 03 (Oasis):** The machine offers the hero a crown and he declines it — the right
  choice with zero sweat — and then a robot dog I'd never met walked him offstage.

### Pulled me forward

A kid who inherited his father's debt discovers his father was a secret engineer who hid the proof that the system is lying — it's about truth versus a rigged machine.
